subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: You are an obstetrics and gynaecology doctor in an early pregnancy clinic. A 32-year-old woman presents following her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. She is distressed and wants to know why this keeps happening and whether she will ever have a successful pregnancy.
Your tasks:
Take a focused history.
Explain possible causes of recurrent miscarriage.
Outline appropriate investigations.
Discuss management and future pregnancy planning.
Recurrent miscarriage refers to repeated pregnancy losses, but the exact diagnostic threshold varies between professional guidelines.

RCOG: traditionally defines recurrent miscarriage as three or more first-trimester miscarriages, which do not necessarily have to be consecutive. Clinicians may investigate after two losses when a pathological cause is suspected.
ESHRE and ASRM: generally use two or more pregnancy losses, although the precise definitions and included pregnancy types differ.

OSCE tip: State the definition used by your local guideline, acknowledge that investigation may be appropriate after two losses, and do not delay assessment simply because the patient has not reached three miscarriages.
Recurrent miscarriage is distinct from repeated ectopic pregnancies and molar pregnancies, which require their own assessment.
Start sensitively because recurrent pregnancy loss can cause significant grief, anxiety and fear about future fertility.
A suitable opening:

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you have experienced several pregnancy losses, and I am very sorry you have had to go through this. I would like to ask some questions about your previous pregnancies and general health so that we can understand what investigations may help. Is that okay?”
Remember to:
Confirm the patient's identity and preferred name.
Ensure privacy and offer a chaperone if an examination is required.
Ask permission before discussing sensitive details.
Use non-judgmental language.
Avoid implying that the patient caused the miscarriages.
Ask whether she would like her partner or another support person involved.

content_groups.group_title: A. History of previous pregnancy losses

blocks.text: This is the most important part of the history.
Ask about each pregnancy separately.

rows: How many miscarriages have you experienced?
Establishes the number of losses.
At how many weeks did each miscarriage occur?
Early versus later losses may suggest different causes.
Were the losses consecutive?
Helps characterize the pattern.
Was an intrauterine pregnancy confirmed by ultrasound?
Helps distinguish miscarriage from pregnancy of unknown location or ectopic pregnancy.
Was a fetal heartbeat ever seen?
Helps establish the pregnancy's documented development.
Did the miscarriage occur spontaneously or after treatment?
Clarifies the clinical course.
Was tissue tested genetically or sent for histology?
May provide clues to chromosomal or molar abnormalities.
Were there any second-trimester losses or painless cervical dilatation?
Raises concern for cervical insufficiency or other later-loss causes.
Were there complications such as fever, severe bleeding or retained products?
Identifies previous complications.

blocks.text: Also establish whether she has had any live births, preterm deliveries, ectopic pregnancies or molar pregnancies.

Important distinction: A history of repeated painless second-trimester losses may warrant assessment for cervical insufficiency and uterine abnormalities rather than treating every loss as a typical first-trimester miscarriage.
Ask about:
Menstrual regularity and cycle length.
Amenorrhoea or irregular periods.
Previous pelvic infections or uterine surgery.
Fibroids, congenital uterine abnormalities or endometrial adhesions.
Previous dilatation and curettage.
Symptoms suggestive of thyroid disease or hyperprolactinaemia.
Previous infertility assessment or assisted conception.
Ask specifically about conditions associated with pregnancy loss:
Thyroid disease.
Diabetes mellitus.
Systemic lupus erythematosus or other autoimmune disease.
Antiphospholipid syndrome or previous abnormal clotting tests.
Previous deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
Hypertension and other significant chronic illnesses.
Current and previous medications, including anticoagulants.
Ask about:
Recurrent miscarriage in close relatives.
Congenital abnormalities or known chromosomal disorders.
Stillbirths and unexplained fetal deaths.
Venous thromboembolism in the patient or close relatives.
Known parental chromosomal rearrangements.
Ask sensitively about:
Smoking and recreational drugs.
Alcohol consumption.
Body weight and recent weight changes.
Occupational exposures where relevant.
Nutritional status and folic acid use.
Emotional wellbeing, relationship support and the effect of previous losses.
Ask:

items: “What do you think may be causing the miscarriages?”
“What worries you most about another pregnancy?”

blocks.text: “What would you most like us to help you with today?”
These questions demonstrate empathy and patient-centred care.

The examination should be guided by the history and clinical presentation. It is not necessary to perform an invasive pelvic examination routinely in every stable patient attending a recurrent miscarriage clinic.
Assess general appearance and vital signs.
Measure BMI.
Look for pallor if there has been significant previous bleeding.
Examine the thyroid if indicated.
Look for clinical features of endocrine disease or systemic autoimmune disease.
Consider examination for signs of venous thromboembolism, autoimmune disease or other systemic illness when the history suggests these possibilities.
Perform when clinically indicated, for example if there is pelvic pain, a suspected pelvic mass or another relevant abnormality.
OSCE statement:
“I would perform a focused general and systemic examination guided by the history. A pelvic examination would be undertaken if indicated, with consent and a chaperone.”
A useful way to organize the causes is by category.
Sporadic chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo are a major cause of early miscarriage.
Occasionally, a parent carries a balanced chromosomal rearrangement, such as a translocation, which can result in an unbalanced embryo.
The likelihood of embryonic aneuploidy increases with maternal age.
An acquired autoimmune disorder associated with pregnancy complications and thrombosis. It is one of the most important potentially treatable causes to investigate.
Septate uterus.
Bicornuate uterus and other congenital uterine anomalies.
Intrauterine adhesions.
Selected cavity-distorting fibroids or other uterine pathology.
Overt hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.
Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.
Other endocrine disorders when suggested by symptoms or clinical findings.
Increasing maternal age.
Smoking, obesity and excessive alcohol consumption.
Some medications or significant medical illnesses.
Selected inherited thrombophilias, although these are not established explanations for most recurrent early miscarriages.
Unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss, even after an appropriate assessment.
Does every woman with recurrent miscarriage have an identifiable cause?
No. A substantial proportion of cases remain unexplained after appropriate evaluation. Many women with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss subsequently have a successful pregnancy.
The purpose of investigation is to identify causes that could change management, rather than ordering every available test.
Request the following antiphospholipid antibody tests:
Lupus anticoagulant.
Anticardiolipin antibodies, IgG and IgM.
Anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies, IgG and IgM.

If results are positive, persistence generally needs to be demonstrated on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart. The diagnosis also requires appropriate clinical criteria; a single positive antibody result does not automatically establish APS.
Lupus anticoagulant testing can be affected by anticoagulant medication, so interpretation may require specialist input.
Depending on the applicable guideline and clinical history, consider:
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
Free T4 if indicated by the TSH result or symptoms.
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies where recommended by the local recurrent pregnancy loss pathway.
HbA1c or glucose testing if diabetes is known or suspected.
Other endocrine investigations, such as prolactin, when symptoms or menstrual history justify them.

content_groups.group_title: C. Assessment of the uterine cavity

blocks.text: Possible investigations include:
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound.
Three-dimensional ultrasound where available.
Saline infusion sonography.
Hysteroscopy when direct assessment of the cavity is indicated.
MRI in selected cases where anatomy remains unclear.
These may identify a septate uterus, adhesions, fibroids or other structural abnormalities.
Depending on the history, available resources and local guidance:
Genetic analysis of pregnancy tissue may be offered to identify chromosomal abnormalities.
Parental karyotyping may be considered after appropriate counselling, particularly where pregnancy-tissue testing or family history suggests a chromosomal rearrangement.
Genetic counselling is important when a parental rearrangement is found.

content_groups.group_title: E. Investigations not routinely recommended for everyone

blocks.text: Do not automatically request:
Broad inherited thrombophilia panels.
Extensive natural killer cell or other poorly validated immune testing.
Routine infection panels without clinical indications.
Routine TORCH screening as a universal explanation for recurrent miscarriage.
Inherited thrombophilia testing may be appropriate for a separate indication, such as a personal or strong family history of venous thromboembolism, or within a specific specialist pathway.
Management should be individualized according to the identified cause, the woman's preferences and local specialist guidance.
Refer to an appropriate recurrent miscarriage or early pregnancy service.
Provide a clear explanation of the investigation plan.
Offer early assessment and appropriate ultrasound support in a subsequent pregnancy.
Acknowledge grief and anxiety; offer psychological support or counselling when wanted.
Avoid making promises about the outcome of the next pregnancy.

rows: Antiphospholipid syndrome
Specialist-directed low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin in pregnancy when indicated.
Overt thyroid disease
Treat and optimize thyroid function before and during pregnancy.
Poorly controlled diabetes
Improve glycaemic control before conception and throughout pregnancy.
Uterine cavity abnormality
Refer for specialist assessment; selected abnormalities may warrant surgery, but the likely benefit and risks must be discussed.
Parental chromosomal rearrangement
Genetic counselling; discuss reproductive options appropriate to the individual situation.
Other medical disorders
Optimize the underlying condition and review medications for pregnancy safety.

blocks.text: APS exam point: Aspirin and heparin are not routine treatments for every woman with recurrent miscarriage. They are used when APS or another appropriate indication is established.

content_groups.group_title: C. Progesterone in a subsequent pregnancy

blocks.text: Progesterone is not a universal treatment for unexplained recurrent miscarriage.
Under the NICE approach, vaginal micronized progesterone may be offered to a woman who has:
Vaginal bleeding in the current early pregnancy.
At least one previous miscarriage.
An intrauterine pregnancy confirmed by ultrasound.

A commonly recommended regimen is 400 mg vaginally twice daily; if fetal cardiac activity is confirmed, the NICE regimen continues until 16 completed weeks. Follow the applicable local guideline and assess the patient for other causes of bleeding, including ectopic pregnancy where relevant.
Advise the patient to:
Stop smoking.
Avoid alcohol during pregnancy.
Aim for a healthy weight.
Optimize chronic medical conditions.
Review medications before conception.
Take routine preconception folic acid, commonly 400 micrograms daily, unless a higher dose is indicated for another reason.
Attend early antenatal assessment in the next pregnancy.

content_groups.group_title: E. If no cause is identified

blocks.text: Explain that no specific drug treatment has been proven to prevent every unexplained miscarriage. Continue supportive care, individualized pregnancy monitoring and a clear plan for prompt review if bleeding or pain occurs.
A good OSCE counselling response might be:
“I am sorry you have experienced these losses. Recurrent miscarriage can be emotionally difficult, and it is understandable to be worried about another pregnancy.

There are several possible explanations, including chromosomal abnormalities, certain autoimmune conditions and abnormalities of the uterus. Sometimes, even after thorough investigations, we cannot identify a definite cause.

We can investigate for conditions that may affect the outcome and treat those where an effective treatment is available. Many women with recurrent miscarriage go on to have a successful pregnancy, although I cannot guarantee an individual outcome.
We will discuss the investigations, make a plan for a future pregnancy and ensure you have access to support. You do not have to go through this alone.”
Advise urgent medical attention if she develops:
Heavy vaginal bleeding, fainting or collapse.
Severe or worsening abdominal pain, particularly unilateral pain.
Fever, offensive vaginal discharge or severe systemic illness.
Significant pain or bleeding in a future pregnancy before the pregnancy location has been confirmed.
These symptoms may indicate haemorrhage, ectopic pregnancy or infection and should not be attributed automatically to her history of miscarriage.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: Example presentation:

“This is a 32-year-old woman with three consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses, consistent with recurrent miscarriage under the three-loss definition. I would clarify the gestational age and clinical documentation of each pregnancy, including ultrasound findings and any genetic results.

My differential aetiologies include sporadic embryonic chromosomal abnormalities, antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine structural abnormalities and endocrine or metabolic disease. I would also assess relevant medical, family and lifestyle factors.

My investigation plan would include antiphospholipid antibody testing, appropriate thyroid and metabolic assessment, evaluation of the uterine cavity and selected genetic investigations where indicated. Management would be directed by the results, alongside sensitive counselling, supportive care and preconception planning.”

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between recurrent miscarriage and recurrent pregnancy loss?

The terms are often used interchangeably, but definitions differ across guidelines. Some definitions focus on clinically recognized miscarriages, while others include a broader range of documented pregnancy losses. Always clarify the applicable guideline.
Q2. What is the most important treatable cause to investigate?
Antiphospholipid syndrome, because selected patients benefit from specialist-directed aspirin and heparin treatment during pregnancy.
Q3. How do you confirm persistent antiphospholipid antibodies?
By demonstrating the relevant antibody positivity on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, interpreted alongside the clinical criteria.
Q4. Should all patients undergo inherited thrombophilia testing?
No. Routine screening is generally not recommended for recurrent early miscarriage alone. Testing may be indicated by a separate thromboembolic history or specialist assessment.
Q5. Should all patients receive aspirin and heparin?
No. These treatments are appropriate for APS and selected other indications, not unexplained recurrent miscarriage in general.
Q6. What is the role of progesterone?

It may be considered in a subsequent pregnancy when the patient has early pregnancy bleeding and a previous miscarriage, with an intrauterine pregnancy confirmed by ultrasound, according to the applicable guideline.
Q7. What is the role of parental karyotyping?
It can identify a balanced chromosomal rearrangement in a parent. It is generally considered selectively, with genetic counselling, rather than assumed necessary for every patient in every pathway.
Q8. How would you respond if the patient blames herself?

Reassure her that miscarriage is rarely attributable to a single action and that many early losses are related to chromosomal abnormalities beyond anyone's control. Acknowledge her feelings without offering false certainty.
Giving a rigid definition without acknowledging guideline differences.
Failing to document the details of each individual pregnancy.
Forgetting antiphospholipid syndrome.
Ordering indiscriminate infection, thrombophilia or immune panels.
Prescribing aspirin and heparin without an appropriate indication.
Promising that a future pregnancy will definitely succeed.
Ignoring grief, anxiety and the patient's support needs.
Failing to give safety-net advice about bleeding, pain and fever.
Embryonic aneuploidy; parental rearrangements in selected cases.
Test appropriately; confirm persistent antibodies.
Assess uterine anatomy and the cavity.
Thyroid disease, diabetes and relevant autoimmune conditions.
Smoking, weight, alcohol and medication review.
Sensitive counselling, targeted investigations and future pregnancy planning.
1. Which condition is a particularly important treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage?
2. How far apart should repeat antiphospholipid antibody tests generally be to demonstrate persistence?
3. Which statement about inherited thrombophilia testing is most accurate?

items: It is mandatory in every patient
It is routinely needed before progesterone

blocks.text: It is generally not recommended routinely for recurrent early miscarriage alone
4. A woman has recurrent miscarriage of unexplained cause. Which is the best counselling statement?

items: She cannot have a successful pregnancy
Aspirin and heparin must be prescribed to everyone
A successful pregnancy remains possible, and supportive care is important
